715.title: The trustworthy
715.hook: Mecca calls him al-Amin and al-Sadiq, the trustworthy and the truthful
715.howItsDone: Muslims refer to the Prophet ﷺ as al-Sadiq al-Amin, the truthful and trustworthy, and honesty in speech and trade is taught as part of following his example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fudul, the pact of the wronged. Your line was: defend the wronged. Did you take your small step for someone treated unfairly? Day seven hundred fifteen.

Some reputations are built by speeches. This one, as the sirah tells it, was built the slow way, in the ordinary dealings of a trading town: what a person says, what a person keeps, what a person gives back. By the time the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ is a grown man in Mecca, the sirah says, people have stopped using only his name. They call him by what he is to them. A title given not by a king, but by neighbors and traders. Today: the trustworthy.
screen: `NOT BUILT BY SPEECHES.` → `SMALL THINGS, DONE THE SAME WAY.` → `A TITLE FROM THE NEIGHBORS.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq says Quraysh called him al-Amin, the trustworthy. Tradition remembers him too as al-Sadiq, the truthful. Two words, one picture: a man whose word matched what happened, and whose hands could be trusted with what wasn't his. Muslims often point to two hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari where the praise comes from people who had turned against his message. The first comes from the day he began to call his own clans in public. He climbs the hill of Safa and calls them by name. When they gather, he asks: if I told you there were horsemen in the valley behind this hill, about to attack you, would you believe me? And they answer: yes, we have never known you to say anything but the truth. Then he tells them his message, and his own uncle Abu Lahab scolds him in front of everyone. But they had already said it. The second comes from Abu Sufyan, at the time still one of his fiercest opponents, standing before the Byzantine emperor Heraclius, who questions him about this new prophet. Heraclius asks: did you ever accuse him of lying, before he made his claim? And Abu Sufyan says no. In the same report he admits he'd have lied about him if he hadn't feared his companions calling him a liar. Heraclius reasons aloud: a man who never lied about people would hardly lie about God. Both scenes come from after the revelation began, but both look back. In them, even his opponents say that before the message, they had known him for his word. The trust was there first.
screen: `AL-AMIN AND AL-SADIQ.` · `"WOULD YOU BELIEVE ME?" AT SAFA.` · `ABU SUFYAN BEFORE HERACLIUS.` · `THE TRUST CAME FIRST.` · then, large: `KNOWN FOR TRUTH.`

segments.voice: The practice: be truthful in one hard moment. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a moment coming up today or this week where the easy thing is a small untruth. An excuse for being late. A compliment you don't mean. A number rounded the convenient way. Picture the moment clearly. Now picture yourself saying the true thing instead, kindly, plainly. Notice what happens in your body. Rehearse the sentence once in your head until it feels like yours. If you pray, you can ask Allah to make your word match your deed. The bell holds the time.
The trustworthy. Al-Amin, what Mecca called him, the sirah says, before any revelation came, and al-Sadiq, the truthful. Today's word.
Your line: known for truth. Today, when the hard moment you rehearsed arrives, say the true sentence, kindly. Day seven hundred fifteen.

716.title: Khadijah's caravan
716.hook: she sends him to Syria with her goods and her servant Maysarah, who returns full of praise
716.howItsDone: Muslims remember Khadijah as a respected merchant and as the Prophet's ﷺ first wife, and honesty in trade is taught from his example and from hadith such as the one on the truthful, trustworthy merchant.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the trustworthy. Your line was: known for truth. When your hard moment came, did you say the true sentence? That closes the childhood and youth. Now, a new part: Khadijah and the household. Day seven hundred sixteen.
screen: `KNOWN FOR TRUTH.` → `NOW: KHADIJAH AND THE HOUSEHOLD.`

segments.voice: A merchant in Mecca has goods to send north, and she doesn't travel with them. Whoever carries them will be out of her sight for a long time, buying and selling with her money in markets far from Mecca. She needs someone she can trust completely, someone who will bring back every coin, and she has heard a name. The merchant is a woman, Khadijah bint Khuwaylid. Today: Khadijah's caravan.
screen: `GOODS TO SEND NORTH.` → `OUT OF HER SIGHT FOR A LONG TIME.` → `A WOMAN OF TRADE.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq describes Khadijah as a merchant woman of honor and wealth, who hired men to trade with her goods for a share of the profit. She has heard about the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: his truthfulness, his trustworthiness, his character. Yesterday's title has traveled. So she sends him an offer. Take my goods to Syria, she says, and I'll give you more than I give the others. And she sends her servant Maysarah with him. He accepts. The caravan goes north. He trades, sells what he brought, buys what she wanted, and comes back to Mecca. The sirah says the business did well. But the profit isn't what the story lingers on. It lingers on Maysarah. Maysarah has spent the whole journey beside him, seeing him far from home: in the heat, at the market, at the haggling table where small dishonesties are easy. When they return, Maysarah goes to Khadijah and tells her what he saw. Ibn Ishaq says his report included wonders: a monk's words about him, and angels Maysarah saw shading him from the sun. That's the turn in this story. The goods came back. So did a report, and it was about the man, not the profit. The Qur'an's word for something handed over like this is amanah, a trust. In surah four, Pickthall translates: "Lo! Allah commandeth you that ye restore deposits to their owners." He restored hers, and more. Later, in a hadith collected by al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet says the truthful, trustworthy merchant will be with the prophets, the truthful and the martyrs. A merchant, in that company. Tomorrow we'll see what Khadijah did with Maysarah's report.
screen: `A MERCHANT WOMAN OF HONOR.` · `"TAKE MY GOODS TO SYRIA."` · `MAYSARAH WATCHES THE WHOLE WAY.` · `THE REPORT WAS ABOUT HIM.` · then, large: `RESTORE DEPOSITS TO THEIR OWNERS.`

segments.voice: The practice: do work you'd be glad to be reported on. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one piece of work you'll do today, paid or unpaid: a task at your job, a chore, an errand for someone, an assignment. Now picture a Maysarah beside you, someone quiet, simply watching how you do it. Not to catch you out; just to see. What would they report? Is there one corner you'd usually cut, one shortcut nobody would notice? Choose, now, to do that part well. If you pray, you can ask Allah for honest hands. If not, just hold the choice. The bell holds the time.
Khadijah's caravan. The trading journey to Syria she entrusted to him, with her servant Maysarah, who came home, the sirah says, speaking of him with wonder. Today's word.
Your line: his honesty was the report. Today, do the corner you'd usually cut, properly, whether or not anyone ever finds out. Day seven hundred sixteen.

717.title: She proposed
717.hook: Khadijah, respected and independent, proposes marriage through a friend
717.howItsDone: Muslims remember Khadijah as Umm al-Mu'minin, a mother of the believers, and her proposal is often retold in talks on marriage and on the dignity of women in the Prophet's ﷺ life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khadijah's caravan: her goods went north to Syria, and her servant Maysarah came home talking about the man who led it. Your line was: his honesty was the report. What did your own work say about you? Day seven hundred seventeen.

A message leaves a merchant's house in Mecca, carried quietly by a friend. It comes from a woman of standing, with her own wealth and her own trade. It goes to a young man with no fortune at all. She has heard Maysarah's report about the man who led her caravan. She has weighed it, and made up her mind. The friend's question sounds casual: what's keeping him from marriage? It isn't casual at all. Today: she proposed.
screen: `A MESSAGE FROM A MERCHANT'S HOUSE.` → `TO A MAN WITH NO FORTUNE.` → `SHE PROPOSED.`

segments.voice: Remember who Khadijah was: the merchant from yesterday, with her own goods on the road and men hired to trade them. She wasn't marrying for money. What she was choosing was a person. In Ibn Ishaq's telling, she sends word to him and gives her reasons herself: the family tie between them, his good name among his people, his trustworthiness, his character, his truthfulness. Not his money; he had little. Her reasons are about who he was. Another report, in Ibn Sa'd, says she first sent a friend, a woman named Nafisa, to ask him quietly what was keeping him from marriage. He said he had nothing to marry with. And Nafisa asked: and if that were taken care of, and you were invited by beauty, wealth, standing and a good match? So the go-between opened the door, and Khadijah walked through it. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told his uncles, and the families met, and the marriage was made. The sources give different names for who spoke for her family; they agree on who asked first. The Qur'an, much later, describes what a marriage is meant to hold. In Pickthall's words: "He ordained between you love and mercy." And there's a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari that answers her choice from the other side. Years on, the angel Jibril comes to the Prophet and says: Khadijah is on her way to you with a dish of food. When she arrives, give her greetings of peace from her Lord, and from me. A woman who chose, and was greeted by name.
screen: `A MERCHANT WOMAN OF STANDING.` · `HER REASONS WERE HIS CHARACTER.` · `A FRIEND OPENS THE DOOR.` · `GREETINGS FROM HER LORD.` · then, large: `SHE CHOSE HIM.`

segments.voice: The practice: honor a strong woman. Settle, and breathe. Bring one to mind. Someone who made a decision others wouldn't have made, and stood behind it. A grandmother, a boss, a neighbor, a teacher, a friend. Picture her face. Then name, quietly, the reasons you trust her, the way Khadijah named her reasons: what she does, how she treats people, what she has carried. Let them be specific. If you pray, you can ask good for her by name. If not, simply hold her in mind with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
She proposed. Khadijah, a merchant of standing, asked the Prophet to marry her, through a friend and with her own reasons, for the sake of his character. Today's word.
Your line: she chose him. Today, tell one strong woman in your life a specific reason you trust her, in a message or out loud. Day seven hundred seventeen.

718.title: Their children
718.hook: Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, Fatimah, and sons who died in infancy
718.howItsDone: Muslims who lose a child say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un and pray for the family; the Prophet's ﷺ name Abu al-Qasim, after a son who died young, is still used of him today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, she proposed: Khadijah, a merchant of standing, asked him herself, for the sake of his character. Your line was: she chose him. Whose strength did you name out loud? Day seven hundred eighteen.

Abu al-Qasim. Father of Qasim. It's a kunya, a name built from a child's name, a way of calling a man through his child. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was called by this one, and it is still used of him today. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari even has him say: call yourselves by my name, but not by my kunya. And Qasim himself? A little boy who did not live to grow up. His father carried his name anyway. Today: their children.
screen: `FATHER OF SO-AND-SO.` → `ABU AL-QASIM.` → `A LITTLE BOY WHO DIED.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq lists the children Khadijah bore him. Sons first: al-Qasim, and then the names al-Tayyib and al-Tahir, the good one and the pure one. Some scholars read those two names as one son, called Abdullah, with two titles; the sources don't settle it. Ibn Ishaq says simply that the sons died before Islam came. And then the daughters, each with her own story still ahead: Zaynab. Ruqayyah. Umm Kulthum. Fatimah. Ibn Ishaq says the daughters lived to see Islam, accepted it, and emigrated with their father. Here traditions read the record in more than one way. Sunni tradition counts all four as daughters of the Prophet and Khadijah. Some Shia scholars hold that Fatimah alone was their daughter by birth, and that the others were raised in the house; other Shia scholars accept all four. And of Fatimah, her father says in Sahih al-Bukhari: Fatimah is a part of me. Put it together and the house in Mecca comes into view. A mother who traded, a father who was trusted, girls growing up, and small graves too. Grief came into that home before any revelation. And the sources keep every name. Even the boys who died small have names on the page and a place in the line. There's one more picture, from a long dream the Prophet describes in Sahih al-Bukhari. He sees the prophet Ibrahim in a garden, and around him, children. He's told they are the children who died young. Every child remembered.
screen: `SONS WHO DID NOT GROW UP.` · `FOUR DAUGHTERS, AND HOW THEY'RE READ.` · `FATIMAH IS A PART OF ME.` · `CHILDREN IN A GARDEN.` · then, large: `EVERY CHILD REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray for children who died young. Go gently. If this is close to you, take only what you can. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a child who didn't get to grow up. Maybe one you knew, or one in your family's story, or a child you only heard about in the news. Say the name if you know it. If you don't, the child is still held. If you pray, you can ask Allah's mercy for that child, and comfort for the people who still miss them. If you don't pray, just keep the name, or the face, in mind. The bell holds the time.
Their children. Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah, and the sons who died small, al-Qasim among them, whose name his father carried. Today's word.
Your line: every child remembered. Today, if you know a family who lost a child, say that child's name to them, or write it down somewhere you'll see it. Day seven hundred eighteen.

719.title: Zayd chooses
719.hook: Zayd, a freed boy in the house, chooses to stay with him rather than go home with his own father
719.howItsDone: Muslims remember Zayd ibn Harithah as a beloved companion of the Prophet ﷺ, and his story is told when teaching about the Qur'an's ruling that adopted children keep their birth parents' names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, their children: four daughters, and little sons who died, al-Qasim among them, whose name his father carried. Your line was: every child remembered. Whose name did you keep? Day seven hundred nineteen.

A father has been looking for his son for a long time. The boy was taken in a raid, the sirah says, and sold in a market far from home. The father mourned him in verse: I weep for Zayd, and I don't know what became of him. Then word comes. The boy is alive, in Mecca, in the house of a man of Quraysh, Muhammad ibn Abdullah. The father and his brother ride south with money to buy him back. They find him. And the boy says no. Today: Zayd chooses.
screen: `A BOY TAKEN IN A RAID.` → `A FATHER WEEPS IN VERSE.` → `THE BOY SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: Here's how the sirah tells it. Zayd ibn Harithah came into the house as a gift. Khadijah's nephew had bought him, she received him, and she gave him to her husband, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. When Zayd's father, Harithah, arrived with the ransom, the Prophet didn't haggle. He said, in the account Ibn Sa'd keeps: call him, and let him choose. If he chooses you, he's yours, with no price. If he chooses me, I'm not a man to turn away someone who chooses me. So they called Zayd. Do you know these men? Yes, my father and my uncle. And Zayd said: I won't choose anyone over you. His father was stunned. You'd choose slavery over your own father and family? And Zayd answered that he had seen something in this man that he would never trade. Then the Prophet took him by the hand to the gathering place by the Ka'ba and said to the people: bear witness, Zayd is my son. And the father, the report says, went home at peace. After that, people called him Zayd ibn Muhammad. Sahih al-Bukhari records that they kept calling him that until a verse came, and Pickthall renders its opening: "Proclaim their real parentage." So he was Zayd ibn Harithah again, his own father's son. But the bond stayed. And the Qur'an itself, at surah thirty-three, verse thirty-seven, mentions Zayd by name. A boy who chose a house, kept in the Book.
screen: `A GIFT IN KHADIJAH'S HOUSE.` · `CALL HIM, AND LET HIM CHOOSE.` · `BEAR WITNESS, ZAYD IS MY SON.` · `HIS OWN FATHER'S NAME RESTORED.` · then, large: `HE CHOSE TO STAY.`

segments.voice: The practice: thank someone who chose you. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a person who picked you when they didn't have to. A friend who stayed. A stepparent. A teacher who took a chance. A partner. Someone who let you choose, and then honored what you chose. Hold their face for a moment. What did it cost them to choose you? If you pray, you can thank Allah for them by name. If not, just let the gratitude sit in your chest a while. The bell holds the time.
Zayd chooses. Offered his freedom and his father's home, Zayd ibn Harithah chose to stay with the Prophet, who then called him his son. Today's word.

720.title: Ali in the house
720.hook: young Ali, Abu Talib's son, is raised in the Prophet's home
720.howItsDone: Muslims who sponsor or care for orphans often recall the Prophet's ﷺ words about the two fingers side by side, and Ali's upbringing in his home is told when Muslims remember Ali.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zayd chose: offered his father's home, he stayed, and was called a son. Your line was: he chose to stay. Who did you thank for choosing you? Day seven hundred twenty.

A hard year comes to Mecca. Ibn Ishaq calls it a severe famine, and says it hit Quraysh badly. One house feels it hard: Abu Talib's. He's the uncle who took in an orphaned nephew years before, gave him a bed and a place at the table. Now Abu Talib has a big family and not enough to feed them. And the nephew, grown now and married to Khadijah, has an idea. Today: Ali in the house.
screen: `A HARD YEAR IN MECCA.` → `ABU TALIB'S HOUSE STRAINS.` → `THE NEPHEW HAS AN IDEA.`

segments.voice: Day seven hundred eleven gave this plan in a sentence. Here it is up close, as Ibn Ishaq tells it. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ goes to another uncle, al-Abbas, and says: your brother Abu Talib has a large family, and you can see how hard things are. Let's lighten his load. I'll take one of his sons, you take one. Al-Abbas agrees. They go to Abu Talib together and ask. So two boys change houses that year. Al-Abbas takes Ja'far. The Prophet takes Ali, a small boy, into his home with Khadijah. Under that roof he joins Khadijah, and Zayd, the boy who chose to stay. A household that keeps making room. Ibn Ishaq says Ali stayed with him from then on, and when revelation came, Ali followed him and believed. Later, the paths read Ali's place in more than one way. Sunni tradition counts him among the rightly guided caliphs; Shia tradition holds him to be the Imam after the Prophet. But here he is still a child at Khadijah's table. Ali wasn't an orphan; his father was alive. The man who took him in had been one, though. And in Sahih al-Bukhari, that man says the one who looks after an orphan will be with him in Paradise like this, and he holds up two fingers side by side. The house that raised Ali was run by someone who knew what that care was worth. Raised in that house.
screen: `A PLAN TO LIGHTEN THE LOAD.` · `TWO BOYS CHANGE HOUSES.` · `A HOUSEHOLD THAT MAKES ROOM.` · `TWO FINGERS SIDE BY SIDE.` · then, large: `RAISED IN THAT HOUSE.`

segments.voice: The practice: care for a child not your own. Settle, and breathe. Think of a child in your world who isn't yours. A niece, a neighbor's kid, a student, a child in a family going through a hard year. Or think back to an adult who did that for you when you were small. Hold that child, or that adult, in mind. Then ask one plain question: what would lighten the load? A meal, a ride, an hour, a book, a kind word to a tired parent. If you pray, you can pray for that child by name. The bell holds the time.
Ali. Abu Talib's young son, taken into the Prophet's own home with Khadijah in a hard year, and raised there. Today's word.
Your line: raised in that house. Today, do one small thing to lighten the load for a child, or for the person raising one. Day seven hundred twenty.

721.title: The black stone lifted together
721.hook: at thirty-five he settles the tribes' quarrel over the stone with a cloak (sirah)
721.howItsDone: Pilgrims circling the Ka'ba pass outside the curved wall of the Hijr, and touch, kiss or gesture toward the Black Stone, following the Prophet's ﷺ example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ali, who in a hard year, Abu Talib's son came to live with the Prophet and Khadijah. Your line was: raised in that house. Whose load did you lighten? Day seven hundred twenty-one.

Before the quarrel, there was a rule about money. The Ka'ba was old and damaged, and the clans of Quraysh agreed to pull it down and build it again. Ibn Ishaq says one of their elders stood up and told them: put nothing into this House but clean money. Nothing earned from usury, nothing from prostitution, nothing taken unjustly from anyone. They agreed. So they gathered only clean money, and built, clan by clan, wall by wall. Today: al-Amin.
screen: `AN OLD HOUSE, DAMAGED.` → `ONLY CLEAN MONEY.` → `CLAN BY CLAN, WALL BY WALL.`

segments.voice: Clean money ran short. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, from 'Aishah, says the Prophet told her that her people's funds fell short, and so a part of the old House was left outside the new walls. That's the space behind the low curved wall on one side of the Ka'ba, the Hijr. Pilgrims circle outside it, because it belongs to the House. The Qur'an remembers who raised the House's foundations. Pickthall's words: "And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House." So the clans of Mecca were rebuilding, imperfectly, something they believed Ibrahim had begun. Then came the corner where the Black Stone sits, and every clan wanted the honor of setting it in place. Ibn Ishaq says the quarrel went on for days, and the clans came close to fighting. They agreed to let the next man through the gate decide. It was the one they called al-Amin, the trustworthy; Ibn Ishaq says he was thirty-five. He asked for a cloak, laid the stone on it, and had a man from each clan take hold of the edge. They lifted it together, and he set it in the wall with his own hand. This closes a week of the household. The trustworthy one. Khadijah's caravan. Her proposal. Their children, every one remembered. Zayd, who chose to stay. Ali, raised in that house. And a cloak with room for every hand. Next comes the mountain, and the revelation.
screen: `CLEAN MONEY RAN SHORT.` · `THE HIJR, LEFT OUTSIDE.` · `A STONE ON A CLOAK.` · `A WEEK IN THE HOUSEHOLD.` · then, large: `EVERYONE A CORNER.`

segments.voice: The practice: solve a quarrel so everyone shares. Settle, and breathe. Think of a disagreement near you, at work, at home, in a group chat, where each side wants the honor or the last word. Don't pick a winner. Picture the cloak instead. What would let every person take hold of an edge? A shared task. A decision made together. Credit spread around. Let one idea come, small and practical. If you pray, you can ask for wisdom in it. The bell holds the time.
Al-Amin, the trustworthy. The name Quraysh called him when the clans feared fighting over the Black Stone, and he set it in place so every clan could lift it together. Today's word.
Your line: everyone a corner. Today, in one shared task, make sure every person has a real piece of it, and say whose hands were on it. Day seven hundred twenty-one.
